name: Fussenbach
title: Nights on the Fussen
tagline: Every real day is one night in Fussenbach, where the river keeps its own hours.

unavailable.scavenge: There is no rubble to sift in Fussenbach. The green is in the silt; take a rake to the basins instead.
unavailable.train: There is no Pit in Fussenbach, and the yard behind the Flagon is not the same.

arrival: {warband} came up the Fussen on a grain barge and took the rooms above the Cracked Flagon. The village noticed, and said nothing.
watchNote: A village of thirteen hundred and one pub. There is no rubble to sift and no Pit to fight in; the basins, the Flagon, the shrine and the wharf will have to do.

blurbs.dredge: Work the algae basins for what glows in the silt. Shards, and the lie of the mudflats.
blurbs.carouse: Drink at the Cracked Flagon, where the village talks once it trusts you. Favour, rumours, a Fortune charm.
blurbs.spy: Listen under the wharf and at the Watch House wall. Rumours and Sight.
blurbs.pray: Keep the candles at Sigmar's Hammer. Blessings, Fortune.
blurbs.trade: Move the green to the bargemen quietly. Market chits; five shards make one.

dredge: The basins were half-worked. The other half of the harvesters are under chalk.
The harvesters worked in cloth masks. The masks did nothing about the smell and nothing about the chalk.
A basin had been chalked off. {first} worked the one beside it and did not ask why.
carouse: Half the Flagon wore cloth over their faces. The landlord served through it.
The Flagon served through the hatch. Nobody came in. Nobody wanted to be the one who brought it.
The landlord's boy had chalk on his sleeve and would not say whose door.
spy: Every second door {first} passed on the lane was chalked. Nobody spoke above a whisper.
The chalked doors were the quiet ones. {first} listened at the unchalked ones and learned who was afraid.
The Watch walked the lane with cloth over their faces. It made them harder to tell apart, which some of them liked.
pray: Father Justinian had run out of candles by the third hour and kept the vigil in the dark.
The shrine was full of the sick, and the spears were stacked by the door for once.
Father Justinian said the rites at three doors before dawn and did not go in to any of them.
trade: The bargeman weighed the coin through a cloth and did not touch it.
The bargemen would not come ashore. The deal was done from quay to deck, sliver for coin, thrown.
The chandler had put his prices up for the chalk moon. Nobody argued. Nobody had the breath.

dredge: A wide hat watched the flats from the mill bridge the whole time.
The hat on the mill bridge wrote something down when {first} pulled up green. {first} wrapped it faster.
The harvesters worked in silence under the hat's eye, and the silence was worse than the smell.
carouse: The Flagon went quiet twice. Both times a hat had come in.
The hat sat in the Flagon's corner and drank water. The whole room drank slower.
The landlord took the fiddle down from behind the bar and put it under the bar. Hats do not like fiddles.
spy: {first} was not the only one listening at the Watch House. The other one had a torch.
The hunters were listening too, and they had a warrant, and {first} had a good pair of boots. The boots won.
A hat asked at the Flagon for anyone who had been under the wharf. The room looked at its ale.
pray: A witch hunter knelt in the front row of the shrine. Father Justinian stopped counting spears.
The hat knelt in the front row and Father Justinian's sermon changed halfway through into something safer.
Every candle in the shrine was lit and nobody would say by whom. The hat wrote that down.
trade: The wharf gate was shut. The deal was done through the bars.
The bargeman would not touch the green while the hat was in the village. The deal was done with a boot on it.
The buyer at the tollhouse paid double and asked {first} to walk back the long way. The hat was on the short way.

dredge: The silt hummed under {first}'s rake. Nobody on the flats stopped to wonder why.
The basins glowed from below like a lit window. The harvesters worked with their eyes shut.
{first} did not need the lantern on the flats. That was the trouble. Nobody needed a lantern.
carouse: The pumpkin ale had a green cast by candlelight. Nobody sent it back.
The Flagon's window glowed green from the wharf side. The landlord drew the curtain and it glowed through the curtain.
The chandler's candles burned green and the chandler sold them anyway and said it was the tallow.
spy: The whole wharf glowed faintly. It made the listening easier and the hiding worse.
Warehouse 4 lit up from beneath like a lantern with the slats for a shade. The mercenaries in front of it cast no shadows.
{first} could read the Watch House rota by the light off the river. It was the wrong rota.
pray: The candle flames burned green for a moment. Father Justinian did not comment.
Father Justinian's candles burned green and he blessed them anyway, and his hand shook doing it.
The hammer over the shrine door caught the river's light and looked, for a moment, like something else.
trade: The bargeman's scale would not settle. He blamed the moon, and then the river.
The green sold itself. The bargeman could see it through the rag and paid before it was unwrapped.
The buyer at the tollhouse held it up to the sky and the sky was the same colour. He paid in a hurry.

dredge: The village was all at the Mud-Gate to see the gibbet. {first} had the flats alone.
The gibbet at the Mud-Gate creaked all night. The flats were silent, which was a change, and not a good one.
The harvesters drank instead of working. {first} worked instead of drinking and had the green to show for it.
carouse: The whole Flagon was drinking to the hanged man. {first} drank to him twice.
The hanged man had drunk at the Flagon for twenty years. His stool was left empty and everyone drank to it.
The landlord's boy told the story of the hanging six times before midnight, and it was a different man each time.
spy: Everyone was talking. It was hard to hear anything for the talk.
The whole village was at the Mud-Gate. The wharf was empty of everyone but the Baron's men, who were loading.
In the crowd at the gibbet {first} heard three names said quietly. Two of them were Watch.
pray: Father Justinian was saying the rites for the hanged. {first} waited a long time for a candle.
Father Justinian would not say the rites for the hanged man. He had known the man. The Baron's men had known him better.
The shrine was empty for once. Everyone was at the gate. Everyone but Father Justinian, who was praying for the hangman.
trade: The chandler did brisk business in the effects of the dead.
The hanged man's boat was sold before he stopped swinging. The bargeman who bought it did not want it. He wanted what was under the boards.
The crowd at the gibbet was the best market of the month. {first} was not the only one who thought so.

dredge: No mill wheel, no barges. {first} could hear each stone turn in the silt.
The mill wheel was stopped for the moon and the mill race ran clear. {first} could see what was in it.
Even the harvesters did not talk. Even the eels did not move. The silt gave up the green like a secret.
carouse: The Flagon spoke in murmurs. Even the dice were quiet.
The Flagon's fiddle stayed behind the bar. The landlord pointed at the ceiling and shook his head.
Nobody sang. Somebody played the table with a spoon and was hushed.
spy: In the silence every word carried across the water.
The mercenaries on the wharf whispered and the whispers carried to the reed beds. {first} was in the reed beds.
The chattering under the shrine floor could be heard from the lane. Everyone in the lane pretended it could not.
pray: Nobody sang. The candles did what candles do.
Father Justinian said the rites in a whisper. The floor answered in a whisper. Neither would give way.
The bell was not rung. The candles were lit in silence. It felt, {first} said afterwards, like waiting.
trade: The bargeman wrote his price on a slate and turned it around.
The deal was done by pointing. The bargeman pointed at the coin. {first} pointed at more coin. The bargeman nodded.
Nobody haggled. Haggling is loud. The prices were fair because nobody dared say otherwise.

dredge: Barge crews were already picking over the shoreline. {first} worked further out.
Half the barges in Ostermark were on the Fussen and half the bargemen were on the flats with rakes.
The harvesters sold basins by the night to strangers. {first} had paid in advance.
carouse: The Flagon was full of bargemen with coin and no sense of how much.
The Flagon ran out of pumpkin ale and served something from Bechafen. Nobody complained and everybody noticed.
The bargemen sang the boat song and got the words right, being bargemen. The village forgave them.
spy: The wharf was loud with strangers. Strangers talk.
Every barge on the Fussen had a story. Most were lies. {first} kept the three that agreed.
The Baron's men checked every barge's papers. One barge had no papers and was not checked.
pray: Father Justinian took a collection at the door. It was a good night for it.
The shrine had strangers in it for once. Father Justinian preached to them about the river. He did not mention the floor.
A bargeman gave the shrine a candle as thick as an arm. Father Justinian lit it and it burned white, and he wept.
trade: There were three buyers for every sliver and the bargeman hated all of them.
Three buyers bid for {first}'s sliver on the quay, and the fourth, who did not bid, paid the most.
The bargemen had coin and no time. The price was whatever was said first.

dredge: The wind had moved the silt overnight. Basins were there that had not been.
Ash lay on the basins like a skin. Under it the silt was warm and the green came up easy.
The harvesters said the ash brought the green down the river. From where, nobody said. Everybody knew.
carouse: Ash from the west came in under the Flagon door and settled on the ale. Nobody minded.
The Flagon's fire would not draw and the room filled with the smell of somewhere else burning.
The landlord wiped ash from the bar between rounds and asked, every time, whose it was.
spy: Footprints in the ash on the wharf told {first} who had passed, and how many.
Ash on the manor road showed three sets of prints going up and two coming down.
The Watch left prints in the ash on the wharf. The mercenaries left none. They had been there since before it fell.
pray: The candles guttered in the draught and had to be relit twice.
Ash came in under the shrine door and Father Justinian swept it into a pot and would not throw it out.
The candles burned with grey flames and the villagers took it for a sign, and were not wrong.
trade: The bargeman wiped ash from the scale between every weighing.
The buyer at the tollhouse asked if the green had come down with the ash. {first} said yes. It paid better.
The bargemen would not moor at the wharf under the ash. The deal was done from a punt, coin passed on a rake.

dredge: Someone had been through the basins already, in a hurry, owing money.
The harvesters were working double to pay the Baron's rent on the basins. There is a rent now.
{first} worked a basin whose harvester was in the Watch House for debt. His rake was still in it.
carouse: Every table in the Flagon was arguing about who owed whom.
The landlord called in what the village owed him and the village paid in pumpkins. The yard is full of them.
The chandler and the miller argued over a debt from the old Baron's time and stopped, both at once, when the old Baron was mentioned.
spy: Debt makes people talk. {first} let them.
The Baron's men were collecting. {first} followed them door to door and counted the doors that did not pay. They were all Watch.
The landlord's boy sold {first} who owed whom for a penny. It was a long list. Captain Hauer was not on it.
pray: The shrine's poor box had been forced. Father Justinian prayed for whoever did it.
Father Justinian owed the chandler for a month of candles. The chandler forgave it in the shrine, in front of everyone, and looked at the door.
The poor box had been emptied and filled again with lead. Father Justinian prayed over the lead as if it were silver.
trade: The bargeman was calling in what he was owed and paid quickly to be rid of the coin.
The bargeman owed the Baron. The green went to the Baron. {first} was paid by the Baron's man, in the Baron's coin, on the Baron's quay.
The chandler paid {first} in credit against candles. Nobody in Fussenbach is short of candles now.

districts: the cliff path below the manor
the wayshrine on the Ostermark road
details: It rained on the river until the third hour.
The fog came up off the silt and did not leave.
The mill wheel stopped once in the night, and started again.
A green cast on the water by the wharf, gone when looked at.
The frogs went quiet all at once.
Sulphur on the wind at low tide.
A light in the manor's upper window, the wrong colour for a candle.
Something big turned over in the river and was not a fish.
The Watch passed twice. Different men each time.
Pumpkin ale on every breath in the lane.
Chains clinked in Morr's Garden with no wind to move them.
The barges were dark. All of them.
A dog would not cross the mill bridge.
Frost on the reeds by dawn.
Somebody was hammering in the shrine after midnight. Not on a nail.
A bell buoy rang on the water, though the village keeps no buoy.
The tide went out further than the old men said it could.
Smoke from the charcoal burners lay flat on the fields.
A cart came down the north road with its lamps out.
The eel-weirs were empty. The eels had gone somewhere.
Something scratched under the floorboards of the Flagon and was ignored.
The manor's dogs barked at the cliff and then, all at once, did not.
Wet rope. Rotting pumpkin. Tallow, from the shrine.
The stars were out over the marsh. The marsh did not reflect them.
A barge slipped its mooring at midnight and was found upstream. Upstream.
The gravedigger's lantern moved through Morr's Garden until the third hour.
Two of the Watch argued at the Mud-Gate in whispers. One of them wept.
Green foam along the tideline in the morning. The gulls left it alone.
The mill ground all night with nobody in it.
A woman sang a lullaby on the ferry stair to nobody.
The reeds moved against the wind.
The manor road had been freshly raked. Something had been dragged along it first.
Ice in the basins, though the river ran free.
A heron stood on the fish-gut quay all night and would not feed.
A rider went north at a gallop with no saddlebags.
The shrine's bell rang once, cracked, and nobody had pulled it.
Bootprints on the causeway going out to the marsh. None coming back.
The Flagon's landlord slept in his chair with the poker across his knees.
Fish came up dead along the upper bends, white-eyed and too many.
The Baron's mercenaries changed the guard on the wharf three times.
A child's shoe on the ferry stair. Small. Nobody claimed it.
The wind came off the river and smelled of a smithy.
The tithe barn was lit from inside. The tithe was paid a month ago.
Somebody had left a pumpkin on every grave in Morr's Garden. Hollowed.
Rats crossed the lane in a line, unhurried, toward the water.
The old tollhouse had a fire in it. Nobody has lived there for years.
The moon came up green over the marsh and corrected itself.
Dawn came late. The mist held it back over the water for an hour.
closers: Nobody spoke of the manor.
The shutters were checked twice.
The river went on saying what it says.
The count was taken at the Flagon's door.
Nobody slept on the side of the house facing the water.
A candle was left burning in the window, for whoever.
The night was not mentioned at breakfast.
The ledger was written with the door barred and the tide going out.
The boots were left outside to drain. Nobody wanted them in.
The landlord said nothing and charged for the ale.
Somebody checked the floorboards before lying down.
The lantern was hung in the window facing the wharf. It was answered.
Nobody said the word rats.
The tide came in and the talk stopped.
The fire was built high and nobody said why.
The knife stayed under the pillow. It has been there since the barge.
Nobody asked where the third bottle came from.
The count was one short until the privy door opened.
The river was listened to for a while.
Somebody went down and barred the Flagon's back door as well.
Father Justinian's bell was heard at the wrong hour and nobody remarked on it.
The pumpkin on the step was thrown in the river.
Nobody slept until the mill wheel started again.
The warband agreed, without saying so, not to walk the manor road.
A coin was left for the landlord's boy. He did not ask what for.
Nobody looked at the water on the way up.
The chain was heard in Morr's Garden and the door was checked a third time.
The ledger was written fast and the candle put out faster.

boon: {name} worked the Dredger's Basins from dusk. The muck gave up two slivers that glowed through the rag they were wrapped in.
{first} waded the silt flats at low tide and came back with green in a jar and a story about a bone with teeth marks that nobody will hear twice.
{name} found where the basin water was warm and dug there. Two slivers, and a fungus that lit the path home.
{first} pulled a harvester's rake through {district} until the tines came up bright. Nobody else on the flats looked up.
{name} took a punt out to the upper bends and dredged where the dead fish float. Two slivers, and the punt is sold.
{first} worked the eel-weirs after the eel-men had gone home. Green in the trap where eels should have been. Two slivers.
{name} dug the drowned orchard at low tide and found the roots wrapped round something bright. Two slivers, and a tree that will not fruit again.
{first} followed the green foam along the tideline to {district} and dug where it gathered. The pockets came back heavy.
{name} dredged the mill race while the wheel stood still. Two slivers from under the paddles, and a look from the miller's window.
{first} worked the marsh causeway by lantern until the lantern was not needed. Two slivers. The light was coming from the ground.
{name} paid a harvester for his basin for the night and got the money's worth twice over. The harvester wants the basin back.
{first} went out on the flats under {omen} and came back with green in both boots. The boots were emptied carefully.
fair: {name} dredged {district} until the light went. One sliver, and a hand that will not get clean.
{first} worked the basins with the algae men. They talk about the tide the way other men talk about debt. One sliver.
{name} sifted the silt below the mill race. One sliver, and something long that swam off when the lantern turned.
{first} came back from the flats with a sliver and a bootful of river. The river was the heavier.
{name} dredged the reed beds. One sliver, small, and a nest of something that had already left.
{first} raked {district} for six hours. One sliver, and the outline of a very large footprint that the tide filled before dawn.
{name} worked a basin the harvesters had given up on. One sliver, and a reason they had given up on it.
{first} dug the fish-gut quay at low tide. One sliver, and a smell that came home too.
{name} dredged below the wharf where the crates are loaded. One sliver, a nail with the Kummerspeck seal, and a mercenary's boot on the ladder above.
{first} pulled a sliver from the eel-weirs and a second thing that looked like one and was a tooth.
{name} worked the drowned orchard. One sliver, and an apple, in Nachexen, from a tree that has no leaves.
{first} dredged {district} with the tide against {them}. One sliver, and the tide won.
{name} went out on the marsh causeway and dug at the edge. One sliver. The bootprints beside {their} own were not {their} own.
{first} worked the silt off the ferry stair. One sliver, and a coin from the old Baron's time, still bright.
{name} took a rake to the upper bends where the fish come up dead. One sliver. The fish had no eyes.
{first} dredged until the mill wheel started again and took that as the signal to stop. One sliver.
poor: {name} dredged {district} until the third hour and brought up bones. Not old ones. Scratched.
{first} went out on the flats and the tide came early. Nothing found. Both boots lost.
{name} worked a basin a harvester had said was good. The harvester had lied, and was not at the sheds in the morning.
{first} dredged the mill race and pulled up a rat the size of a dog. It was not dead enough.
{name} raked the reed beds and raked up a hand. It was wearing a Watch ring. Nothing green.
{first} worked {district} in the fog and worked the wrong way. Came back on the far side of the river, somehow, with nothing.
{name} dug below the wharf and was seen by the Baron's men. The rake is theirs now. So is the night.
{first} went to the basins and found them drained. Somebody had let the water out. Somebody had let something else out.
{name} dredged the eel-weirs and brought up eels. Just eels. Too many eels, moving as one.
{first} worked the upper bends and the punt took on water that was warm. Nothing found. The punt was left where it sank.
{name} dug at the drowned orchard and the ground moved back. Nothing green. Nothing said.
{first} spent the night in {district} up to the knee in silt that did not want to let go. It let go at dawn, reluctantly, with nothing in it.
standing: {name} worked the usual basin in {district}. The usual green, the usual smell.
{first} took the rake to {district} out of habit and came back out of habit.
{name} dredged the usual stretch below the mill. The mill did not comment.
{first} went out with the harvesters and came back with them. A harvester's night.
{name} raked {district} until the tide said stop. It said stop early.
{first} worked the flats as usual and came home as usual, smelling of it.

boon: {name} drank at the Cracked Flagon until the bargemen forgot {they} were a stranger. By the last candle they were telling {them} which crates not to look at.
{first} bought the Flagon a round of pumpkin ale and was forgiven for it. The village knows the name now.
{name} held the corner table at the Flagon against three watchmen and a miller. The miller paid.
{first} sang the Ostermark boat song at the Flagon, badly, and was made to sing it twice. That is how the village says welcome.
{name} out-drank the chandler, which nobody has done, and was given the chandler's stool, which nobody has sat on.
{first} lost at dice to the landlord's boy on purpose and won the landlord for it. There is a room going free above the bar.
{name} drank with the charcoal burners, come down from the woods for the night. They do not talk to villagers. They talked to {first}.
{first} told a Mordheim story at the Flagon and the room stopped to hear the end. The end was worth a round, and the round was worth a name.
{name} matched the eel-men cup for cup. The eel-men drink like they fish: silently, and all night. {first} is an eel-man now.
{first} played the fiddle that hangs behind the Flagon's bar. It had not been played since the old Baron's wake. The landlord wept and charged nothing.
{name} sat with the algae harvesters until they stopped drinking to forget and started drinking to remember. {first} remembers all of it.
{first} bought Captain Hauer a drink and Captain Hauer drank it, in front of everyone. The half of the Watch that matters noticed.
fair: {name} sat at the Flagon and let the room get used to {them}. The room took its time. A fair night.
{first} drank with the algae harvesters at the Flagon. They drink to forget the basins. {first} drank along.
{name} lost two hands of dice to a bargeman at the Flagon and won the third. Honour even, purse lighter.
{first} found the Flagon's back room. A watchman was in it who should not have been. Nothing was said.
{name} drank at the Flagon with the miller's apprentice, who has been told not to talk and nearly did.
{first} bought a round for the ferry-men. They drank it and nodded. From ferry-men that is a speech.
{name} stood at the Flagon's bar for four hours and was served without being asked {their} name. Progress.
{first} played skittles in the Flagon's yard until the lantern went out. Lost, mostly. Was asked back.
{name} drank with two of the Watch who were off duty and very careful to say so. They said so five times.
{first} sat by the Flagon's fire and listened to the landlord's boy tell the story of the mill wheel. It gets longer every night.
{name} was stood a drink by a stranger in grey oilskins who asked nothing and left. The drink was good. The silence after it was not.
{first} traded a Mordheim story for a Fussenbach one. The Fussenbach one was shorter and worse.
{name} drank at the Flagon while the rain came down the chimney. Nobody moved. That is what the Flagon is for.
{first} let the chandler win at dice and the chandler knows it. It will be useful. It may be expensive.
{name} drank pumpkin ale until it tasted of something. That took a while.
{first} sat in the Flagon's window and watched the wharf while pretending to drink. The landlord pretended not to notice. Fair all round.
poor: {name} drank at the Flagon and the room went silent when {they} asked about the manor. It stayed silent.
{first} came back from the Flagon without {their} purse and with a mercenary's opinion of strangers.
{name} asked the wrong bargeman about the wharf. The bargeman left. So did the warmth in the room.
{first} drank alone at the Flagon. The landlord kept wiping the same glass.
{name} was outdrunk by the chandler, like everyone, and put to bed in the chandler's yard, like most.
{first} laughed at the wrong moment in a story about the old Baron. The story stopped. So did the evening.
{name} tried the Flagon's back room and found two of the Baron's men in it. Left by the window. The window was not open at the time.
{first} drank with the eel-men and was sick in the eel-men's boat. They have long memories and short tempers.
{name} sang the boat song with the wrong words. In Fussenbach the words matter. The ale stopped coming.
{first} called the pumpkin ale what it is. The village knows what it is. The village does not want to hear it from a stranger.
{name} fell asleep at the Flagon's corner table and woke with a rat chalked on the table in front of {them}. Nobody saw who did it.
{first} was asked, politely, whether the strangers would be moving on soon. Then asked less politely.
standing: {name} kept the usual stool at the Flagon. The usual pumpkin ale.
{first} drank at the Flagon and was neither welcomed nor asked to leave.
{name} sat where {they} always sit. The landlord poured without asking.
{first} drank two and went home. The village barely noticed. That is the point of a village.
{name} kept the Flagon's corner warm. Nobody argued for it.
{first} drank at the Flagon in the usual silence. Companionable, by now.

boon: {name} lay under the wharf at low tide for four hours and heard the mercenaries count crates. The count did not match the manifest.
{first} followed a lantern from the Mud-Gate to the manor road. It went in by the kitchen door and did not come out.
{name} paid a dredger's child a penny in {district} and got three rumours. Two are true. The third is worse.
{first} sat below the Watch House window where Captain Hauer keeps his ledger. Somebody else's ledger was being argued about.
{name} lay in the reeds by the eel-weirs and watched a barge unload at the wrong quay, into a cart with no driver.
{first} climbed the cliff path below the manor and lay under the study window until the light changed colour. It changed twice.
{name} spent the night in the tithe barn's loft. Two of the Watch met below to divide silver. They divided it three ways.
{first} followed the gravedigger through Morr's Garden and watched him unchain a headstone, wait, and chain it again. Something had knocked.
{name} sat in the charcoal burners' camp and let them talk. They talk about the woods. The woods have been walking.
{first} listened at the chandler's back door and learned who is buying the candles Father Justinian is not. It is the manor.
{name} counted the mercenaries on the wharf by their pipe-glow. Eleven. The Baron pays for six.
{first} found the young guardsman the whole Watch is looking for. {first} is the only one who has. {first} has not said where.
fair: {name} listened at the shrine door. Father Justinian was not praying. He was counting spearheads.
{first} watched the {rival} from the mill bridge. Somebody there was watching back.
{name} traded a rumour for a rumour at the ferry stair. Fair exchange. Both about the river.
{first} learned which of the Watch take the wharf road at midnight and which take the long way. It may be useful. It may be why.
{name} sat in the Flagon's window and counted who left by the back. Half a name and a direction.
{first} lay on the tithe barn roof and watched the north road. One rider, no lamps, going up. None coming down.
{name} listened under the Watch House floor. The floor is thin. So is the peace.
{first} watched the eel-men at their weirs. They do not fish after the third hour. They wait.
{name} followed the miller's apprentice to the water and back. He goes to look. He does not know what for.
{first} learned the manor's kitchen takes delivery at midnight, from a cart that comes down the cliff path, which has no road.
{name} paid the landlord's boy a penny for who sleeps in the Flagon's back room. A different watchman every night. The same silver.
{first} watched the algae sheds and saw the harvesters carry something out under a sack. It was the shape of a man. It moved.
{name} lay in the pumpkin fields and heard the {rival} argue about the manor road in whispers. They agreed on nothing.
{first} sat in the wayshrine on the Ostermark road and counted carts. Four went to the village. Two came back heavier.
{name} listened at the boatyard. Somebody is building a very long box with a chain on it.
{first} got a name from the ferryman for the price of a crossing. The name was Hauer. The direction was down.
poor: {name} was seen on the manor road. Not stopped. Seen, from an upper window.
{first} listened at a warehouse door in {district} for two hours. It was Warehouse 3.
{name} followed a mercenary through the fog and found the mercenary was following {them}. Both went home.
{first} spent the night in {district} learning that nobody in Fussenbach talks under {omen}.
{name} lay in the reeds until the reeds were the ones listening. Left quickly. Learned nothing but that.
{first} was caught on the cliff path by the manor's dogs. The dogs did not bark. That was worse.
{name} hid in the tithe barn and was found by the gravedigger, who did not ask, which was worse than asking.
{first} listened at the Watch House wall and heard {their} own name. Nothing else. That was enough for one night.
{name} followed a lantern to Morr's Garden and lost it among the stones. The lantern is still out there somewhere. So is whoever.
{first} paid a child for a rumour and got the same rumour {they} had sold the child last week.
{name} was seen by two of the Watch, and the two of the Watch were the wrong two.
{first} watched the wharf all night and saw nothing, because the fog was arranged that way.
standing: {name} kept an ear open at the Flagon. Nothing worth the ink.
{first} watched the wharf from the usual stair. The usual lanterns.
{name} listened at the usual wall. The wall said the usual things.
{first} sat where the lane meets the water and counted the Watch. The usual number.
{name} kept the usual corner. Nobody came to it.
{first} listened out of habit and heard the river out of habit.

boon: {name} kept the candles at the Shrine of Sigmar's Hammer until dawn. Every one of them held. Father Justinian noticed, and asked nothing, which is rarer.
{first} knelt in the shrine until the stone hurt. Something answered from below the floor. {first} chose to call it Sigmar.
{name} lit a candle for each of the village's drowned. Father Justinian brought a second box. There were still enough.
{first} prayed at the shrine with the door open onto the fog. Nothing came in. That was the answer.
{name} kept the vigil with the villagers who have new spears, and when the chattering came from below, {first} was the one who kept praying. They noticed.
{first} walked to the wayshrine on the Ostermark road and back before dawn. The candle carried the whole way and did not go out.
{name} said the rites over an unmarked grave in Morr's Garden because nobody else would. The chain on the next stone went slack.
{first} prayed on the mill bridge for the dead in the river. The wheel stopped for the length of it. The miller did not complain.
{name} sat with Father Justinian while he sharpened, and prayed while he did not. By dawn he had stopped sharpening.
{first} lit a candle in the shrine and the chattering beneath the floor stopped, and stayed stopped, and the villagers looked at {first} differently.
{name} blessed the ferry at the ferryman's asking. It is the first blessing he has asked for in thirty years. He did not say why.
{first} kept the candles under {omen} and felt, for one moment, the whole village praying with {them}, in their beds, without knowing it.
fair: {name} kept the candles at the shrine. They held until the third hour, and the chattering under the floor stopped when they did.
{first} sat with Father Justinian and said little. The priest kept looking at the door.
{name} prayed at the shrine and felt watched over. Or watched. The village does not distinguish.
{first} lit one candle in the shrine and it did not go out. Take that as given.
{name} said the words at the wayshrine on the Ostermark road. A cart stopped, and the driver said them too, and drove on faster.
{first} prayed at the Flagon's table before drinking, which nobody in Fussenbach does. Two others did it after.
{name} helped Father Justinian count the candles. He counts them the way Captain Hauer counts his men. Neither count comes out right.
{first} knelt in Morr's Garden at low tide and the chains were quiet. A blessing or a coincidence, and the gravedigger says he does not care which.
{name} kept the vigil and heard the floor. Did not stop. Did not look down. That is what the vigil is now.
{first} prayed for the bargemen who did not come back. Nobody knew their names. Sigmar presumably does.
{name} lit candles at the shrine and a villager asked {them} to bless a spear. {first} did. It was not the first spear that night.
{first} sat in the shrine while Father Justinian slept in his chair for the first time in a week. Somebody had to.
{name} said the rites on the ferry stair for a child's shoe. Nobody claimed it. Somebody wept from a window.
{first} prayed at the shrine and the candle flames leaned toward the floor. Only for a moment. Only once.
{name} kept the candles and Father Justinian talked, for once, about the old Baron. He stopped himself. Then he prayed harder.
{first} knelt until the doubt and the prayer were about even. In Fussenbach that counts as faith.
poor: {name} kept the candles at the shrine. The draught off the river took them one by one.
{first} prayed at the shrine and heard only the mill wheel. It is possible the wheel was the answer.
{name} went to the shrine and found it full of villagers holding new spears. Stood at the back. Left early.
{first} knelt in {district} until the doubt was louder than the prayer, and the frogs louder than both.
{name} lit a candle in Morr's Garden and the wind put it out. There was no wind.
{first} prayed at the wayshrine and found somebody had scratched the hammer off it. Recently. With claws.
{name} went to the shrine and Father Justinian asked {them}, gently, to come back another night. There were men in the vestry. They were not praying.
{first} kept the vigil and fell asleep, and dreamed of teeth, and woke with the candles out and the door open.
{name} prayed on the mill bridge and the wheel jammed as {they} said amen. The miller looked at {them} for a long time.
{first} lit a candle for the old Baron and it burned green to the socket. Father Justinian took the stub and did not give it back.
{name} knelt in the shrine and the chattering below was louder than the words. Stopped praying. Started listening. That was the mistake.
{first} prayed at the shrine and a villager asked whether Sigmar could hear them this far from anywhere. {first} did not have an answer. That was the night.
standing: {name} lit the usual candle at the shrine. It burned as usual.
{first} said the words at the shrine. Father Justinian nodded without looking up.
{name} kept the usual candle. The floor was quiet, as usual, or as usual as it gets.
{first} prayed at the usual hour. The village has started to set its clocks by it.
{name} knelt in the usual place. The stone has a mark now.
{first} said the usual words. They are still the right ones.

boon: {name} met a bargeman below the wharf and let the silence do the haggling. The bargeman broke first and threw in a warning.
{first} moved the green in {district} to a man who paid too well and asked where the Kummerspeck seal was. There was no seal. He paid anyway.
{name} sold a story at the Flagon's back table along with the goods. The story fetched more.
{first} found a buyer in {district} who owed the {rival} money. Interesting rates. Interesting silence.
{name} traded with the charcoal burners, who pay in silver nobody has seen in the village. Old silver. The old Baron's face on it.
{first} sold to an alchemist's man at the old tollhouse who counted out coin without looking at it. He was looking at the north road.
{name} moved the green through the ferryman, who takes a tenth and asks nothing. Tonight he took a tenth and gave a name.
{first} traded at the boatyard with a shipwright who wanted the green for the wood, not the coin. The wood does not rot with it in. The wood glows.
{name} met a buyer at the wayshrine who paid in Altdorf coin and left toward the village. The village does not know he is coming.
{first} sold to the chandler, who does not deal in the green, at a price the chandler does not offer. The chandler has a new customer and is frightened of him.
{name} did the deal under {omen} on the fish-gut quay with a bargeman who kept looking at the water. He paid double to be done quickly.
{first} let a buyer think the green was from Warehouse 4. The buyer paid Warehouse 4 prices. The buyer will find out.
fair: {name} traded on the lower docks. Fair weight, fair price, and a look over the shoulder for both parties.
{first} spent the night at the ferry stair arguing over a sliver with the chandler. The chandler enjoyed it more.
{name} came back from {district} with less green and more coin. The coin was Ostermark-minted, and recent.
{first} watched a bargeman weigh everything twice by lantern. The second weighing was for the mercenary on the quay.
{name} sold at the old tollhouse to a man who did not get down from his cart. Fair price. The cart smelled of vinegar and something under it.
{first} traded with the eel-men, who pay in eels and coin in a ratio they will not explain. Fair, probably.
{name} did business at the boatyard. Fair weight. The shipwright kept the scale away from the water.
{first} sold a sliver to the miller's apprentice for the miller. The miller does not know. The miller will.
{name} traded in the Flagon's yard by the light from the window. A fair chit, and the landlord's boy watching from the woodpile.
{first} met a buyer on the marsh causeway who paid fair and walked off into the marsh. There is nothing in the marsh.
{name} moved the green through the gravedigger, of all people. He pays fair. He does not say where it goes. Down, presumably.
{first} argued price with a bargeman until the tide turned. The tide decided it. Fair.
{name} sold at the tithe barn to a man who counted coin onto the tithe chest. The chest was open. It was not empty.
{first} traded a sliver for a chit and a second chit for the sliver back. Came out ahead by the width of a chit.
{name} did the deal on the ferry, mid-river, where nobody can listen. The ferryman listened.
{first} traded on the lower docks and was paid in coin with the Baron's seal filed off. Fair weight. Somebody was in a hurry.
poor: {name} went to the wharf to trade and found Rudolf's men on the gate and no bargemen anywhere. Nothing taken but the night.
{first} was offered a price in {district} that was an insult and a warning at once. Took the long way home thinking about which.
{name} traded in {district} and got a chit stamped with a seal nobody in the village will discuss.
{first} waited at the ferry stair for a buyer who never came. His barge was there. He was not.
{name} went to the old tollhouse to trade and found the buyer's cart, the buyer's horse, and the buyer's hat. In that order. Nothing else.
{first} was paid in coin that turned out to be lead with a wash of silver. The Baron's face on it, which is either a joke or a message.
{name} did a deal on the fish-gut quay and the buyer dropped the sliver in the water. Something took it before it sank.
{first} traded with a charcoal burner who paid, took the green, and asked {first} not to come to the woods again. Kindly. Firmly.
{name} waited at the boatyard for the shipwright, who has gone upriver, according to the Baron's men. His tools are still on the bench.
{first} found a buyer and the buyer found two of the Watch. The wrong two. The green is evidence now.
{name} sold to the chandler and the chandler sold to the manor, and the manor's men came asking where the chandler got it. The chandler said.
{first} traded at the tithe barn and was paid from the tithe chest. The tithe is the Elector's. The Elector will not hear of it, which is the problem.
standing: {name} kept the usual arrangement on the lower docks. The usual coin.
{first} traded at the ferry stair the way {they} always do. The bargeman nodded.
{name} moved the usual sliver through the usual bargeman. The usual tenth for the ferryman.
{first} did the usual deal in the Flagon's yard. The landlord's boy watched, as usual.
{name} traded with the eel-men as usual. Coin and eels, as usual.
{first} kept the arrangement. The arrangement kept {them}.

pairs: {other} waited at the ferry stair with a lantern and did not light it.
{other} came back first and checked the shutters twice.
The two of them did not speak on the manor road. Nobody does.
{other} kept watch on the lane. A Watch patrol passed and pretended not to see.
{other} was already at the Flagon when {first} came in, and had kept a seat, and had not said for whom.
The two of them met on the mill bridge at the third hour without arranging it.
{other} walked {first} home along the water and neither looked at it.
{other} had the door open before {first} knocked.
They came back by different lanes and arrived at once. The village noticed. The village notices.
{other} was on the ferry stair when {first} came up it, and said nothing, and that was a kindness.
{other} had a fire going and two cups out. The second cup was not asked about.
The two of them counted each other in at the door. Both were there. It is not always certain.
encounters: {rivalMember} of the {rival} was on the wharf too. Nods were exchanged. Nothing else was.
On the way home {first} passed the {rival}'s lodgings. A light was on. Somebody there is also not sleeping.
{rivalMember} of the {rival} had been at the Flagon an hour earlier, asking the same questions. The landlord said so, and nothing else.
The {rival} had left a mark on the mill bridge. {first} added one beneath it.
{first} and {rivalMember} of the {rival} reached the ferry stair from opposite ends. Both waited for the other to leave first.
A boy ran a message between the two lodgings after midnight. Neither warband will say what it said.
{rivalMember} of the {rival} was on the marsh causeway coming back as {first} went out. {rivalMember} shook {their} head. {first} went out anyway.
The {rival} had a man on the tithe barn roof. {first} had the loft. Neither mentioned the other to anyone.
{first} found {rivalMember} of the {rival} asleep in the wayshrine and left {them} asleep. It will be remembered, one way or the other.
The {rival} were at the Flagon's corner table. {first} took the window. The landlord served both and charged neither for the silence.
{rivalMember} of the {rival} dropped a chit on the ferry stair. {first} picked it up and handed it back unread. Probably unread.
The {rival} had been to the shrine first. Their candles were still burning. {first} lit {their} own beside them.
On the manor road {first} met {rivalMember} of the {rival} coming the other way, fast. {rivalMember} said one word. It was 'don't'.
{first} and {rivalMember} of the {rival} hid from the same Watch patrol behind the same wall. Nobody laughed until the patrol had gone.
The {rival} sent a cup of pumpkin ale across the Flagon. {first} drank it. It was not poisoned. That is the state of things.
{rivalMember} of the {rival} was buying the same candles from the same chandler. The chandler raised his prices for both.
The {rival} had a lantern on the mill bridge signalling to somebody upriver. {first} counted the flashes. Four. Then dark.
{first} came home to a pumpkin on the step, hollowed, with a candle in it. The {rival}'s doing, or the village's. The village does not do jokes.
rumours: The crates that leave Warehouse 4 at midnight glow through the slats. The bargemen who mention it stop turning up.
Baron Rudolf has not opened his shutters since Nachexen began. The light in his study is the wrong green.
The gravediggers chain the headstones in Morr's Garden. Ask them what the chains are for and they say the damp.
Something chatters under the shrine floor during the vigil. Father Justinian says it is the cold. He has started buying spears.
Two vagrants who slept by the Mud-Gate are gone. The watchmen on that shift are the ones who take the Baron's silver.
The mill wheel jammed again. Whatever it jammed on had more legs than a fish and fewer than it started with.
The algae men will not work the lower basins after dark. The bones they pull up have teeth marks, and the teeth were not small.
The old Baron was hale on the Feast of Ulric and dead by the next moon. Nightshade, the cook says. Then the cook says nothing.
Somebody walks Morr's Garden at low tide in the old Baron's coat. The coat was buried with him.
Captain Hauer has a young guardsman locked in the Watch House for his own safety. Half the Watch wants the key.
Three men in grey oilskins asked at the Flagon for a guardsman by name. They were not from the village. They paid in Altdorf coin.
The {rival} were seen on the manor road after curfew. They came back faster than they went.
Under the docks at high tide something feeds on the fish-guts. The fishermen throw the guts further out now.
An alchemist's cart came down the north road, went to Warehouse 4, and left heavier than it came.
The Baron's mercenaries are paid on the wharf on Marktag. Eleven queue up. The Baron's ledger says six.
Father Justinian has stopped burying the village's dead in Morr's Garden. He says the ground is full. It is not full.
The shipwright at the boatyard was asked to build a long box with a chain on it. He asked what for. He has gone upriver.
The eel-men will not fish past the third hour. Something fishes the weirs after that, and it is cleaner about it than they are.
The young guardsman who found the Baron's manifests is called Anselm. Half the village says he has already left. The other half saw him yesterday.
Warehouse 4 has a cellar. Warehouse 4 was built on silt. There should be no cellar.
The charcoal burners say the woods above the village have been walking. Trees that were here are there. They have stopped cutting near the cliff.
The old Baron's cook was let go a week after the funeral, with a purse she did not earn and a story she will not tell.
Captain Hauer sleeps in the Watch House with the door barred against his own men.
The chandler sells more candles to the manor than to the shrine. The manor has no window lit but one.
The dead fish along the upper bends have too many fins. The children collect them. The mothers burn them.
The tithe barn has been lit at night for a week. The tithe went to the Elector a month ago, or was meant to.
The mill's apprentice saw a face in the wheel. The miller says it was his own reflection. The apprentice is not that ugly.
The Kummerspeck seal has been seen on crates in Altdorf, in an alchemist's yard, glowing through the slats.
A rider goes north from the manor every third night and comes back every fourth. Nobody in the village rides.
The gravedigger has started digging graves before anyone dies. He says it saves time. He has dug four.
The {rival} asked the ferryman the price of a crossing for eight, with baggage, at night. The ferryman said no price. He did not say no.
Three of the Watch have new boots. Watch pay does not buy boots. The boots are Altdorf leather.
The Baron has not been seen outside the manor since the old Baron's funeral. The manor's servants have not been seen outside since Nachexen.
Something walks the marsh causeway at low tide, in a coat, and turns back at the edge of the village every time.
The green foam on the tideline came as far as the Flagon's step this morning. The landlord swept it into the river. It swam.
Father Justinian has a list of names in the vestry. Not the dead. Not yet.
A grey-coated man asked the chandler for Anselm by name and paid for the answer in advance. The chandler took the coin and lied, he says.
The harvesters found a door in the lower basin at the lowest tide of the year. Iron. New. Locked from the other side.
The old Baron's coat was buried with him. His hound was buried with him. Both have been seen. Separately.
The Baron's study light is green because he reads by a lamp that burns what he sells. That is the kind explanation.
Captain Hauer sent a letter to Bechafen by the Ostermark road. The rider came back without it, or with it, or not at all, depending who you ask.
The {rival} have been buying rope. A great deal of rope. Nobody buys rope in Fussenbach; the river takes it.
There is a second Watch rota, kept by the Baron's men, and the honest half of the Watch is not on it.
The mill ground by itself on Wellentag. The miller found flour in the morning that nobody had milled and would not sell it.
return: The room above the Flagon smelled of pumpkin and river. Somebody had left a candle in the window.
The tide had been in and out a dozen times. The village had not counted.
The landlord nodded as if they had been gone an hour. In Fussenbach that is affection.
The Flagon's boy had kept the room aired and the candle lit, and had charged it to somebody. Nobody asked whom.
The village had decided they were gone and rearranged itself around the gap. It rearranged back without comment.
The tide had left something on the step. It had been taken away again by something else. The step was clean.
cityProvides: A bone charm on the step, wrapped in dried algae. No note.
A dredger's child hands over a folded paper at the ferry stair and runs.
Under the door at dusk: a bargeman's chit, its seal scratched out.
The landlord's boy leaves a charm on the pillow and will not say who sent it.
Wedged in the shutter at dusk: a chit on bargeman's paper, weighted with a stone from Morr's Garden.
A harvester at the Flagon pushes a wrapped thing across the table and goes back to his ale without a word.
Father Justinian's hand, at the door, briefly. Something small in it. Then the door again.
Found in a boot in the morning. Nobody in the room admits to it. The boot was inside the barred door.
quiet: The door stayed barred. Nobody went out. The river went on without them.
A night in above the Flagon. The fire held. The count was taken.
The door stayed barred. The mill wheel could be heard all night, and once, something else.
Nobody went out. The landlord's boy brought up the supper and looked at the shutters and went down again.
A night in. The rain came off the river and nobody missed being out in it.
The door stayed barred. The river rose, and fell, and the count at dawn was the count at dusk. That is a good night here.
